# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. Just watched Blade Runner (1982) for the first time. And i thought it was the most amazing film I've ever seen. Granted I havent watched that much but this takes the cake.

**Score:** 107
**Body:** I'm wondering, since I'm just starting out what are more films that have this grand striking art style and world. Im not necessarily talking about just the "cyberpunk" aesthetic im talking about just cool artstyles, worlds and story telling in general. Maybe things that have impact cinema like blade runner too? Hope my rambling wasn't too confusing lol.

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Brazil
2. You might want to check out Ridley  Scott's first movie, The Duellists (1977). Harvey Keitel, Keith Carradine. Set around the time of the Napoleonic wars. Some incredible photography and story telling.
  - Fantastic film.
3. Different genre, same director - but not for the faint of heart: alien (the original)
  - This for that same world building and immersion. 
4. The Thirteenth Floor. Gattaca. Dark City. A.I. (2001)
5. 2001: A Space Odyssey

Alien

Blade Runner 2049 I guess

Close Encounters of the Third Kind 

To be fair, though, it’s really tough to measure up to Blade Runner
6. You should give The Cell (2000) a watch maybe. Certainly not as impactful, but definitely visually striking and grand.

You've probably seen The Matrix (1999), but give it 20 more years and it will have similar patina to Blade Runner.

Very similar in many ways is 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968), even though it's very differently paced - visually striking and very impactful.

Alien (1979) was a bit like this, thanks to the design by Giger - that started showing up in all sorts of places. And Sigourney Weaver's role was very fresh as well.

Another striking, but not as impactful film would be Sin City (2005) and in a similar space Renaissance (2006).
7. Please watch Blade Runner 2049.


8. Metropolis (1927)

## 2. Just watched Inception for the first time, mind blowing, best movie I've ever seen. What do I watch next after this masterpiece?

**Score:** 60
**Body:** Honestly, everything about Inception was perfect, the visuals, the dream within a dream concept, and the plot twists completely blew my mind. I'm looking for high budget sci-fi movies or psychological thrillers with a similar vibe that will keep me guessing until the very end. Thanks!

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Shutter Island
  - Came here to say this, happy to see it posted!!
2. 12 Monkeys (1995)
3. Have you seen The Prestige? It’s another Christopher Nolan masterpiece. 



The same goes for Interstellar.
  - Add Memnto for that as well, and the prestige is great of course as well. Now where was I?
  - And Memento

Also Vanilla Sky is good.  (not a Nolan movie)
4. Predestination isn't as exciting but it will melt your brain
5. MEMENTO
6. Paprika, since Nolan pretty much adapted it into Inception 
7. Some other “mind-blowers”

Predestination  
Annihilation  
The Prestige  
Children of Men  
Sorry to Bother You  
The Menu  
Upgrade  
Triangle  
Coherence

Edit: adding “The Substance”

## 3. Movies like 12 Angry Men

**Score:** 48
**Body:** Like the title says, I want movies where characters talk a lot, negotiate, deliberate with each other. There should be minimal location change, no action, but engaging and exhilarating at the same time. 

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Glengarry Glen Ross
  - Pretty much any movie based on a stage play will fit what OP is looking for. 
2. Rope (1948)
3. The Man from Earth (2007) it’s exactly what you’re looking for 
4. Margin Call.
5. Conspiracy (2001).


The Wannsee Conference (a '84 German film, with English subtitles).
6. Conspiracy (2001).

Can't recommend it enough.
7. *A Man For All Seasons* (1966), Henry VIII era costume drama. While not an accurate depiction of Thomas More, his character serves well as a spokesman in defense of the rule of law, especially when the nation's leader or ruler demands collaboration and consensus from a legislative body to defy the law. The movie and theater play become significant again every couple of decades.

*Becket* (1964), another superb costume drama, also on the conflict between autocracy and representative government and independence of church and state.
8. My dinner with Andre
9. Witness for the Prosecution, perhaps? Was released that same year as well.

## 4. best movies about loneliness?

**Score:** 44
**Body:** By loneliness I don’t mean not having a romantic partner, but rather not having any friends. Usually, when I’d look up films about this particular theme, I’d mostly find ones that talk about being unable to find a significant other. Meanwhile, having little to no friends is a hardly discussed topic, at least from what I’ve seen.  
So, any suggestions?

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Taxi driver
2. Sideways 
3. The Station Agent (2003). The movie that brought  Peter Dinklage into popularity. It has it's own gentle humor and sympathy. Loneliness, isolation  and also warmth over misery. It's a good film.
4. Not to sound pretentious, but it really is a movie about solitude and not loneliness - Perfect Days
5. Sometimes I Think About Dying (2023)

 
6. The Elephant Man
7. Manchester by the sea
8. *Clockwatchers* (1997) is about a group of young women who all work as office temps together, and while they are friendly at work- they all keep one another at arm’s length and never fully connect. i think it does a wonderful job of illustrating how you can still be lonely and isolated even with surface-level friendships, and how people close themselves off from one another.

*May* (2002) is a horror comedy about a young woman who was bullied her entire life for having a lazy eye. as an adult she is severely socially inept and struggles to connect with others, to disastrous end.

*Welcome to the Dollhouse* (1995) is a bleak dark comedy about a young girl named Dawn Wiener who is bullied everywhere she goes and has no friends.

*Muriel’s Wedding* (1994) wonderful comedy about a very awkward young woman who is obsessed with ABBA and disliked by her peers. the film largely focuses on her developing a meaningful friendship, but she starts out without one.

*Ingrid Goes West* (2017) absurd comedy and social commentary on social media, influencers, and persona. a lonely and grieving young woman moves to California to stalk her favorite influencer and try to become her best friend.
9. Her (2013)
10. Harold and Maude. 



## 5. What horror movie was so intensely terrifying you could only watch it once?

**Score:** 28
**Body:** I am planning a huge horror movie marathon for tonight and need the absolute best recommendations to keep me up all night. I really want to avoid cheap jumpscares and focus on films that build deep tension or have crazy psychological twists. Please explain why your choice is a must watch for a marathon. Thanks!

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Exorcist 
2. Bring Her Back
3. Threads (1984)

The most horrifying film I've ever seen. Probably not good for a fun horror night though.
4. Hereditary. But maybe that's because I'm a parent.
5. The only horror movies that really scare me are ones that convincingly deal with stuff like demons, possession, and hauntings. Trilogy of Terror is a 1980s movie with a possessed Zunni fetish doll that wrecked me when I saw it as a kid. The Wailing is by the same director as Ex Huma (which is also great), and Korean shamans battling demons with knives just won’t have the same magic if you watch it twice.  
6. The French Martyrs
7. Antichrist, but I don't think I even understood the deeper meaning.
8. The Wolf House (La Casa Lobo) 2018

Ive always hated stop motion lol. That, combined with the real life parallels and the ultra surrealism was very unsettling
9. No such film reall but here are some interesting ones. 

Dagon - Good time to watch it. Nightmare material. Lovecraftian though. 

The Descent (UK) - Filled with claustrophobia 

Kuroneko - Ghosts, Samurai, Jungle

Spoorloos - Filled with dread. Psychologically disturbing

Pulse (2001) - Filled with existential dread and grim atmosphere. 
10. I found Sinister deeply unsettling. There were some cheesy parts but the overall feel was so dark and uncomfortable.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. "Why do movies look like that now?" - on the Loss of Light and the new washed out flatness of the moving image

**Score:** 139
**Body:** [Why do movies look like that now?](https://www.avclub.com/why-do-movies-look-like-that-now-contrast-washed-out-cinematography-netflix) << good article here

>*This confluence of consumer trends and changes in production workflow has effectively resulted in frames that strive less for innovation or beauty and more for a quick fix. The quickness and disposability here has infiltrated the set. This means that, outside direct-to-streaming films and the glut of plasticky Marvel and grim DC movies—and exceptions to the rule, like star DPs Roger Deakins, Autumn Durald Arkapaw, and Robbie Ryan—the late 2010s and 2020s have seen the screen get grayer. Regardless of the quality of the movies, their visual identity is constricted by a notable lack of oomph, an absence of substantiality in their colors, highlights, and blackpoints.*

>*The industry, from the best to the worst to the mediocre middle, has gravitated towards a look that takes the wrong lessons from House Of Cards‘ darkness and its low-contrast monotone. Cinematographer Steve Yedlin tells The A.V. Club that “It’s a business, and a lot more stuff gets created than is necessarily the pinnacle of the craft. There is a factory belt.” Felipe Vara de Rey describes the contemporary look as “desaturated, low contrast, a little dull,” Rikki Porter says she’s seen “a more flattened look across the board,” Tara Violet Niami says that movies lately have a “super low-contrast, desaturated look that’s lit softly but \[with\] directionless lighting,” and camera operator Joe Brady says he had been seeing images where “the contrast ratios are very slim \[and\] there’s no detail in the shadows or in a really overexposed highlight.”* 

As a lover of film, sometimes moving from contemporary films and shows to films of the past there is almost a kind of "finally a good steak" when watching films of the past. They not only are satisfyingly structured by the movie making process in terms of story-telling, the way you actually follow what is happening and join into it, they are *visually* structured. There is a visual language. The light itself speaks and illuminates the brain in a much more edifying way. It could very well be that I grew up seeing things that way on the various screens I've been exposed to in my life, and my brain is just used to it, I know how to read those signals, or, it may be that those past processes actually gave enough "meat" for the brain to chew on, in a much more satisfying way. We won't really know until the youth growing on on today's screen aesthetics, themselves turn to older films. Will they too feel that same sense that they are finally sinking their teeth into something visually (even though they were not raised on it)?

Also, one cannot really avoid the sense that everyone consuming pictorial information on very diverse screens, watching films or cuts of films (sometimes accelerated 1.5 or 2x) in the palm of their hands really has altered even what watching a film is or does. Is today's language even a language anymore, but rather just leaning towards a series of style templates and effects meant for consumption and the spread of screens?

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. One thing I’ve been told about the flattened lighting is that now it’s become increasingly common (with Ridley Scott being one notable example) to shoot from multiple angles simultaneously to save time on the day and so that editing decisions can be made more quickly and easily. But shooting for multiple set-ups simultaneously means that you can’t light for a particular set-up, and instead have to wash everything out with light. Which is why everything kind of looks like an old sitcom now
  - Yes, the article mentions that the proliferation of cameras is a big part of this.
2. Actors can't be happy with this. Camera angles and lighting matter so much for appearance and performance.

I suppose that as a viewer, these changes are easy to absorb without question. Most of the new films that I watch are horror, and I've noticed in a lot of them that I feel like it's difficult to see. I had assumed that this was deliberate--it's scary when you can't tell what you're looking at. But a few nights ago I watched Richard Stanley's Dust Devil for the first time in years, and visually, it was ambrosia. Every single shot had depth and design. It really gave me the feeling that I've been missing something in film lately.
  - I watched the 2025 I Know What You Did Last Summer and was pleasantly surprised at how colorful it was for a new horror movie. The summer look was refreshing after a lot of the recent movies I've seen looked muddy or flat 
3. I would add that a big proponent of this is video quality/clarity. Lighting is just as much used to bring clarity to a shot so that you can fully see what's intended, and was very meticulously used for that purpose back in the day. Better video quality now allows us to more easily process visual imagery without lighting, or even intentionally so (for suspense) - e.g. seeing things move in a dark room. So maybe better video quality has spoiled filmmakers into investing less time/energy into lighting?
4. Lighting was one aspect of films I've always looked forward to analyzing. One of my favorite films that gets elevated by dramatic lighting  is Flatliners (1990). At the time of release, the lighting was so over-the-top and absurd. But look up any still from that movie now and it looks so awesome.

Thats a great example of a run-of-the-mill movie that is elevated by awesome lighting choices. Obviously, there are classics like Third Man and Blade Runner that everyone can appreciate.

I hope there comes a day where fun lighting makes a comeback
  - I love La Dolce Vita's lighting. It makes a black and white film feel so colorful.   
That and, of course, The Godfather. Just such rich blacks. 
5. A tale of two movies:

Teenage mutant ninja turtles was filmed in 1989 on a soundstage in North Carolina with pickups in New York on 35 mm film. The production company created the mutants using puppets, animatronics, and humans wearing rubber masks. They masked their unreality with careful camera work, lighting, and discretion. The result is a movie where all the elements feel physically real.

Teenage mutant ninja turtles (2014) shit on a soundstage in California with pickups in Alabama and New York using digital cameras. The turtles are played by human actors wearing motion capture prosthetics. The turtles themselves are a digital simulacrum. Everything onscreen had to be controlled to creates the right conditions for rendering them. There are no clever camera tricks. It's CGI fakery. Our brains know that.

Movies look the same because they're shot on facilities that are purpose built to manage digital production rather than physical assets. Elements like lighting, misc en scene, and composition all serve digital tools. 

>Also, one cannot really avoid the sense that everyone consuming pictorial information on very diverse screens, watching films or cuts of films (sometimes accelerated 1.5 or 2x) in the palm of their hands really has altered even what watching a film is or does.


It isn't the audience's fault.
  - >Our brains know that.

It is an interesting thing. I can watch a Hitchcock film with a CLEARLY filmed backdrop of a car moving through countryside and not for a moment feel like it isn't real, because I can "see" it isn't real, but my brain doesn't bother with that. The situation is real, and that's what matters. Or, I can watch Fast and the Furious "n" and be dulled out with "realistic" effects.

>It isn't the audience's fault.

Wasn't blaming the audience. Only saying that the mode of consumption affects how the product is made. Fast Food was made to eat in a car...when people started eating in cars.
6. This is a trend. Filmmakers decide in pre-production how the film will look. Digital cameras have made it easier to shoot faster due to shooting flat but that doesn’t necessarily affect the lighting. You still have to light a scene. They are choosing how to light a scene. These decisions result in the digital sludge. It’s not due to a fix it in post mantra, which is actually a misunderstanding of the process when that term is often used, nor a lack of competency by the DP.

Films could easily look more vibrant even shot flat. They simply choose this particular look. A small factor may be costume and set design where everything is now browns and blacks with hardly any primary colors.

The final reason, imho, is the trend towards realism. Muted colors appear to audiences, and they lap it up, as more realistic. Audiences are now interested in the “immersive” aspect of film possibly more and consistently than any other era. I believe someone on this very thread already referenced this trend.

Who knows how long this trend will last but it can easily stop when filmmakers make that decision.

## 2. 'The Invite' (2026) is fantastic.

**Score:** 63
**Body:** Looks like Olivia Wilde is back in style after a weak outing with "Don't Worry Darling". Her direction adds so much spark to a film which could have faltered given it's restricted setting and characters. The movie is an adaption of a Spanish film called 'The People Upstairs' and it is like a theatrical play. Just 4 people socializing in an apartment for 2 hours. But the movie never lets go of  its high kinetic energy until the final few minutes, which comes with putting 4 contrasting personalities and 2 contrasting couples together.
The most impressive part to me was how the conversations and dialogues were written. How much they accomplished with such a limited scope. The script is indeed praiseworthy because all the film has is conversations between these 4 people. They are naturally written and seemingly mundane things with bits of humor sprinkled in. But they flow really smoothly from one conversation to the next. 
There may be few off moments occassionally, where the viewer may be taken out, but on the whole you do actually feel these are 4 real people here. You do pick up on hints on the character backgrounds, sometimes very loud sometimes subtle, but the final 10-15 minutes give you a proper insight into the characters.
 I feel the final minutes could have been better written though. The film makes a sudden shift in tone and drama which felt at odds with the rest. There maybe was a way to get the same message across while keeping the spirit the same as before.
As for the ending itself, it is a nice note to end on. Adds depth to a film and gives the viewer something to talk about as they leave.
SPOILERS BELOW:
I think there are two ways to read up on the ending but I think hints are left that it may not be a sad ending after all.
- First of all, Penelope and Edward are real. Just as they leave we see Wilde's character pick up the casserole container and put it down even after they have left. We hear the container being put down which was brought by Penelope thereby hinting that the container was indeed real so was the one who brought it. 
- Secondly, the Penelope (who is now a real person) advises them to understand that the marriage has ended and go their separate ways. And then importantly, she says something along the lines of "or continue the relationship with new versions of yourself". This seems like the biggest hint, because it's not a normal advice someone gives.
- Thirdly, Seth playing the keyboard/piano in the end shows he is changing himself already. This may be a new version, one which has come to terms with his past and is looking for a fresh start.
- Fourthly, the final image of Wilde resting on Seth's shoulder and both close together may have different meanings but the obvious one is that love is still there for each other.
Lastly shoutout to all 4 actors. Perfect casting I say. Seth is really settling into a good actor who can do drama and comedy with ease. Norton is the best here, not too showy but gets his complexity across and Wilde is awesome too. Her range of expressions here in this film is just hilarious and impressive.
Great film tbh, I'd give it a 9/10.

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Top five movie of the year for me so far. The use of space was fantastic. I often find myself getting bored with the limitations of shooting in one location, but this never felt stifled in any way. Also love that the ending is open to interpretation. One burning question though: did Hawk perform cunnilingus or not?

I thought he definitely did. It was just *cunnilingus interruptus*.  

Agreed: really good movie.
  - Agreed on how they used the space. It helped that the apartment was very spacious. Also the kinetic energy of the conversations really kept the audience invested at all times.

They were both pretty tough watches as they highlighted that i really need to change my ways if i want us to get better and back to how we were. I think only good movies like these can make you reflect on yourself and your life and i hope for more in the future

I also took the ending as positive, although I guess there are two ways it could be positive - >!but my interpretation was that the relationship was on the up again. We see, at the end, at least one of the blockers being removed after all!<.
4. It really bums me out that so many of the people who would love this film will refuse to watch it because Seth Rogen is in it. The guy gets a bad rap. This is probably his best performance. 
5. check out the like 5 remakes and original. It's kinda wild seeing so many takes on the exact same story. So far this one has been my favorite because I think they go through the best course of emotion/action.

## 3. The 20 Greatest Films (Positif)

**Score:** 65
**Body:** In 1991, the French film magazine Positif (one of two major French-language film magazines, created several months after Cahiers du Cinema) conducted a poll of the greatest films and published this modest top 20 list…

## 4. Sunrise: A Song of Two Humans (1927)

**Score:** 11
**Body:** A post in r/criterion led me to this beautiful, moving film by F.W. Murnau. Acclaimed by cinephiles as a masterpiece, alas, I had never seen it. 

The arts are the modes of creation allotted to man; be thankful each day you wake up, that you are given anew the opportunity to experience some measure of the greatness that our human race can aspire to. 

*Sunrise* is the famed German filmmaker's first U.S. film. It stars Janet Gaynor and George O'Brien, two popular and busy American actors, as a simple but happy, young (did I mention very attractive?) country couple living with their infant son lakeside in an Old World village.

Ah, but a serpent has slithered into this bucolic Eden. Margaret Livingston plays the alluring high-fashion hottie from the city taking the country air in an elderly peasant couple's humble vacation home rental. The temptress has been seducing the handsome young husband and convincing him to sell the farm, lure his wife into a drowning (dark!), and come wallow in the city's fleshpots with her. 

It almost works. The husband convinces his wife, who knows he's been unfaithful, to take their dinghy for a day away from the farm. She gaily accepts the outing, but it is soon anything but pleasant. Her glowering husband is rowing like Charon on the River Styx, then he comes toward her to throw her in the water. He stops himself, but once they reach the shore his wife jumps out of the boat and runs up into the mountain village, and he chases her to the trolley and boards with her, desperate to make amends and mend his broken vows.

Aside: When they are running through the mountain hillsides, I'm thinking, this looks like the mountains I grew up with in So Cal; yep, much of the exteriors were shot in Lake Arrowhead. 

For the sake of setting the story's narrative, I have neglected the stunning cinematography that opens the film from the scaffolding of a bustling train station, then powers that narrative throughout. Camera “tricks” abound, and the skill and patience to work the analog (pre-analog?) process is a feat of magical proportions. 

Sets were built and lighting engineered to place the actors in the congestion of a 1927 cosmopolitan street with horse-drawn lorries, trolleys, automobiles, pedestrians and pushcarts. Their last day in the city has our dear couple dodging the traffic against a pretty convincing backdrop of the hectic street. They embrace and appear to stop traffic, including a big black horse that pulls a “Frau Blucher” nearly on top of them, then immediately the scene is live, the horse is balking, horns are honking, angry motorists are shaking their fists, and they are pushed out of the middle of a modern maelstrom as they dash off, laughing. 

It's a silent film, so the story is told visually; the actors emote to the balconies, the gags are sight gags, from pie-eyed piglets to the peek-a-boo of a lady's slippery gown strap. 

My favorite, and a wish-I-thought-of-that, is our reunited couple in a photography studio waiting for their prints. They are country clumsy and knock over things. They are horrified when they appear to have broken the head off a classical statue. The search everywhere, under furniture, for the missing head. The husband see a doll's head with some toys and sticks it on the statue – of Winged Victory.

While rowing home, a fearful storm whips up and the boat founders at sea. The husband ties bundles of rushes, stashed for his own escape, to his wife as floatation devices as he endeavors to get to shore, but she goes overboard. The village is roused, rescuers take to the lake. 

The city woman thinks this is her plan at work when the wife is missing. She goes to the devastated husband but he chases her out and starts to strangle her. Then the wife is recovered from the lake! She lives! 

The city woman leaves the village in the back of a horse-drawn wagon down the path in another breathtaking interior. *Finis*

The cinematographers, Karl Struss and Charles Rosher, won the first Oscar for their craft when the Academy Awards were inaugurated in 1929.

## 5. My reading of Dead Poets Society (a 5 year experience)

**Score:** 7
**Body:** When I first watched Dead Poets Society at 10, I hated the ending. I hated Neil's character and how easily he gave up on his dream and on life itself. I thought it was a failure of imagination. Succumbing to death rather than fighting his parents, seeking comfort from his friends, or even running away. Anything, for the sake of just trying.

But five years later, at 15, do I really understand? I don't think there is any character I see my reflection in more.

His tragedy isn't that he doesn't love life or acting. It's kind of the opposite. He loves something deeply in a world that has convinced him that loving it is unacceptable.

Sometimes there truly is nothing left to do. We can pretend things took place differently. In another life, his parents understood. His friends helped him. He decided to wait just a little longer. But the story will continue to end the same.

We always only hear "to speak or to die," as if it's one or the other. But for him, it was both.

"I was good. I was really good."

But often, to speak in itself means to die.

I just hope that understanding it doesn't mean becoming him.
